ASAS-SN describes Sky Patrol light curves as public and provides publication citations. CTAS may link an operator to the official HTTPS coordinate-query page. No automated provider-data request was sent. The official legacy HTTPS query form requires reCAPTCHA and says users needing more than 100 light curves should contact ASAS-SN. The published V2 client and documentation currently use an unencrypted HTTP API, while the linked HTTPS V2 host and client repository are unavailable. CTAS therefore withholds automatic ingestion until ASAS-SN publishes a current secure, bounded machine-access contract. This is an interface-integrity boundary, not a claim that the public light-curve data are proprietary.

rules.classification: Spectroscopic classes and alert or messenger labels are different definitions and are not compared; two active classes differ when neither label refines the other (for example 'SN Ia' and 'SN Ia-91T' agree); an earlier value from the same provider is a revision.
rules.host: Two proposed hosts agree when their names match after case and spacing are ignored or one name is among the other's NED cross-identifications; otherwise they are an identity ambiguity. Association probabilities are not computed.
rules.photometry: Only exactly compatible photometry (same epoch, band, system, method, calibration and direct/difference state, two or more providers) is compared. The limiting magnitude or flux that a provider reports alongside a detection is that epoch's detection threshold, not a non-detection, and is not compared with the detection; a detection brighter than another provider's non-detection limit at the same epoch is a status conflict. A group is listed only when it is still inconsistent under these rules; at most 10 groups per event, most significant first.
rules.position: Two positions with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they are more than 2 arcsec apart; when one states an error radius, the separation is compared with 3 times that radius.
rules.redshift: Two redshifts with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 0.005 (about 1,500 km/s); transient and host redshifts are different definitions and are listed, not compared; host redshifts of differently named hosts are an identity ambiguity.
rules.revision: A retracted row, or a superseded row of the same provider whose value differs beyond the property's rule, is a revision or retraction; a revision within the rule is consistent; the earlier value stays visible.
rules.sigma: Two values that both state an uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 3 combined standard deviations (uncertainties added in quadrature; a stated position error radius is treated as one standard deviation).

persistedQueryReceipts.scope: The anonymous AVSpec search interface explicitly searches published observations. Only rows returned by that interface and anonymously downloadable from the matching official record identifier are eligible. AAVSO states that its hosted data may be used in publications when the current Data Usage Guidelines are followed.

AAVSO states that International Database observations are freely available to the community for research and publication subject to its current Data Usage Guidelines. The v2 JSON API requires token authentication for access; authentication is not treated as a grant of proprietary rights. Only exact target-name and bounded date results from the documented photometry endpoint are eligible.

Only public ADS bibliographic metadata is retained. CTAS does not download, mirror, or assert reuse rights for article full text; publisher and repository links retain their own access and reuse terms. Event association requires an exact retained transient name.

ASAS-SN describes Sky Patrol light curves as public and provides publication citations. CTAS may link an operator to the official HTTPS coordinate-query page. No automated provider-data request was sent. The official legacy HTTPS query form requires reCAPTCHA and says users needing more than 100 light curves should contact ASAS-SN. The published V2 client and documentation currently use an unencrypted HTTP API, while the linked HTTPS V2 host and client repository are unavailable. CTAS therefore withholds automatic ingestion until ASAS-SN publishes a current secure, bounded machine-access contract. This is an interface-integrity boundary, not a claim that the public light-curve data are proprietary.

Official registered public forced-photometry service. ATLAS requires Tonry et al. (2018), Smith et al. (2020) for transient time-domain science, Shingles et al. (2021) for the web service, and the current acknowledgment published on the official forced-photometry home page.

The adapter uses ESO's anonymous TAP service only and retains a reduced-product row only when obs_release_date is present and no later than the query time. ESO states that the proprietary period protects raw and derived data until release and distributes archive data under CC BY 4.0 with acknowledgment requirements. No product bytes are downloaded.

Gaia DR3 is a public ESA data release and ESA identifies CDS as an official Gaia partner data centre. This anonymous adapter is allowlisted to the VizieR copy of catalogue I/355/gaiadr3, stores catalog rows and provider links only, and does not query unrelated VizieR collections or retrieve DataLink products.
Each retained row passed a mission-specific past-release check; XMM also required data_in_heasarc=Y and NICER required VALIDATED. No file bytes were downloaded.

The adapter is anonymous and restricted to the provider-documented public AllWISE Source Catalog and 2MASS Point Source Catalog. It stores catalog rows and official links only; proprietary/exclusive-access IRSA holdings are outside the allowlist.
Only observation and product rows explicitly marked PUBLIC are retained. Product bytes remain provider-hosted; this system stores metadata and official download links only.
NED host queries require one unambiguous host identity; transient coordinates are not silently substituted.

The anonymous public NED TAP service documents programmatic cone searches of the NED Object Directory and requests NED acknowledgment. CTAS retains bounded source-native rows and provenance only. NED states that high-volume automated access is best-effort, so this adapter is single-threaded, starts at most one request per second, and never queries proprietary or user-account holdings.

NOIRLab's provider-owned API authentication notebook states that anyone may retrieve public files while proprietary-file retrieval requires authorization. This adapter sends no credential and retains a product only after an exact file-metadata lookup supplies a nonblank release_date no later than the query time. Anonymous metadata about unreleased files is counted only for exclusion and is never stored. Product bytes are not downloaded.

Rubin alert packets are world-public with no proprietary period, and Fink documents its LSST Science Portal and REST API as real-time, public services requiring no login. Coordinate and first-detection proximity are not proof of source identity.

SIMBAD documents free access without registration under the ODbL license. This adapter uses the anonymous official TAP service for one bounded coordinate query, retains provider attribution and source bibcodes, and does not treat a nearby literature object as the transient, its host, or a new detection.

The official TNS 2.0 API manual documents an object-level public field and a per-spectrum public field. Only an object explicitly marked public=1 and spectrum rows explicitly marked public=1 are normalized. Photometry rows are refused because the current response does not supply a per-row public/private marker.

WISeREP's official help states that private data require a personal API key for scripted access. CTAS sends no credentials, requests public=yes explicitly, and accepts only rows independently marked public=1 from the anonymous public export.

A zero result means ALeRCE holds no public ZTF alert object at this position in the window; it is not a forced-photometry nondetection. Public ZTF alert photometry served by the ALeRCE broker. Cite Förster et al. (2021), AJ 161, 242, and acknowledge ALeRCE and the Zwicky Transient Facility according to current provider guidance.
A zero result may reflect public-release latency or catalog non-detection; it is not a forced-photometry nondetection.

comparison.claimBoundary: Source assertions shown side by side with stated comparison rules. A consistent label is not proof that the values are scientifically equivalent, an inconsistent label is not a judgement of which source is right, and a selection is a display rule, not a measurement or a review.

properties.label: Position

compat.reason: The reference row for this table (the first active row).

properties.rule: Two positions with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they are more than 2 arcsec apart; when one states an error radius, the separation is compared with 3 times that radius.

selections.label: selection, not a measurement
selections.reason: Chosen by ctas-headline.v1 (naming-authority); the source rows are unchanged.
selections.rule: The most recent TNS hourly-feed position (the IAU Transient Name Server is the naming authority); otherwise the GCN localization with the smallest stated error radius; otherwise none.

set.explanation: Every assessed pair is consistent under the stated rules.

rules.classification: Spectroscopic classes and alert or messenger labels are different definitions and are not compared; two active classes differ when neither label refines the other (for example 'SN Ia' and 'SN Ia-91T' agree); an earlier value from the same provider is a revision.
rules.host: Two proposed hosts agree when their names match after case and spacing are ignored or one name is among the other's NED cross-identifications; otherwise they are an identity ambiguity. Association probabilities are not computed.
rules.photometry: Only exactly compatible photometry (same epoch, band, system, method, calibration and direct/difference state, two or more providers) is compared. The limiting magnitude or flux that a provider reports alongside a detection is that epoch's detection threshold, not a non-detection, and is not compared with the detection; a detection brighter than another provider's non-detection limit at the same epoch is a status conflict. A group is listed only when it is still inconsistent under these rules; at most 10 groups per event, most significant first.
rules.position: Two positions with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they are more than 2 arcsec apart; when one states an error radius, the separation is compared with 3 times that radius.
rules.redshift: Two redshifts with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 0.005 (about 1,500 km/s); transient and host redshifts are different definitions and are listed, not compared; host redshifts of differently named hosts are an identity ambiguity.
rules.revision: A retracted row, or a superseded row of the same provider whose value differs beyond the property's rule, is a revision or retraction; a revision within the rule is consistent; the earlier value stays visible.
rules.sigma: Two values that both state an uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 3 combined standard deviations (uncertainties added in quadrature; a stated position error radius is treated as one standard deviation).

runs.claimBoundary: A ranking of retained catalogued galaxies under stated priors; the most probable candidate is a suggestion for follow-up, not a host identification, and a host fainter than the catalogues or outside their cones is always possible.

rules.missed: a host not in the retained catalogues counts as one candidate at f = missedFractionalOffset
rules.offset: f = separation / directional light radius (SIMBAD shape), else separation x kpc/arcsec(z) / physical scale, else separation / angular scale; term exp(-f); f > maxFractionalOffset gives 0
rules.probable: the top candidate is 'probable' when its posterior >= probablePosterior and >= probableRatio x the next hypothesis
rules.redshift: only when the transient and the candidate both have a redshift: exp(-0.5 (dz / sigma)^2), sigma^2 = sum of the stated errors^2 + floor^2

warnings: some candidates have neither a retained shape nor a redshift; their offsets use the stated angular scale

Exact retained ZTF alias ZTF25abovchf; the complete response is kept. Fink science-module scores from the public Fink ZTF API; cite Moller et al. (2021), MNRAS 501, 3272 and include the current Fink acknowledgment.
Each retained row passed a mission-specific past-release check; XMM also required data_in_heasarc=Y and NICER required VALIDATED. No file bytes were downloaded.
Only observation and product rows explicitly marked PUBLIC are retained. Product bytes remain provider-hosted; this system stores metadata and official download links only.
Official anonymous NED API response with NED acknowledgment retained.

Rubin alert packets are world-public with no proprietary period, and Fink documents its LSST Science Portal and REST API as real-time, public services requiring no login. Coordinate and first-detection proximity are not proof of source identity.

Authenticated access to public broker output; token was sent only in the header. Measurements are retained as difference photometry. Lasair public ZTF broker light-curve output. Cite Smith et al. (2019) and the current Lasair acknowledgement requested by the provider.

The official TNS 2.0 API manual documents an object-level public field and a per-spectrum public field. Only an object explicitly marked public=1 and spectrum rows explicitly marked public=1 are normalized. Photometry rows are refused because the current response does not supply a per-row public/private marker.

WISeREP's official help states that private data require a personal API key for scripted access. CTAS sends no credentials, requests public=yes explicitly, and accepts only rows independently marked public=1 from the anonymous public export.

ZTF alert difference-image PSF photometry; non-detections are retained as upper limits, not forced photometry. Coordinate association does not assert identity. Public ZTF alert photometry served by the ALeRCE broker. Cite Förster et al. (2021), AJ 161, 242, and acknowledge ALeRCE and the Zwicky Transient Facility according to current provider guidance.

These are released catalog measurements, not alert difference photometry and not forced photometry. Coordinate association does not assert identity. Public ZTF data-release light curves served by NASA/IPAC IRSA. Cite the ZTF survey/data-release papers and acknowledge IRSA according to current guidance.

selections.reason: Chosen by ctas-headline.v1 (naming-authority); the source rows are unchanged.

set.explanation: Every assessed pair is consistent under the stated rules.

properties.label: Proposed host galaxy

compat.reason: The reference row for this table (the first active row).
Differently named hosts (WISEA J160316.91+030043.9 vs PGC3092347); they may be aliases or different galaxies.

properties.rule: Two proposed hosts agree when their names match after case and spacing are ignored or one name is among the other's NED cross-identifications; otherwise they are an identity ambiguity. Association probabilities are not computed.

rules.classification: Spectroscopic classes and alert or messenger labels are different definitions and are not compared; two active classes differ when neither label refines the other (for example 'SN Ia' and 'SN Ia-91T' agree); an earlier value from the same provider is a revision.
rules.host: Two proposed hosts agree when their names match after case and spacing are ignored or one name is among the other's NED cross-identifications; otherwise they are an identity ambiguity. Association probabilities are not computed.
rules.photometry: Only exactly compatible photometry (same epoch, band, system, method, calibration and direct/difference state, two or more providers) is compared. The limiting magnitude or flux that a provider reports alongside a detection is that epoch's detection threshold, not a non-detection, and is not compared with the detection; a detection brighter than another provider's non-detection limit at the same epoch is a status conflict. A group is listed only when it is still inconsistent under these rules; at most 10 groups per event, most significant first.
rules.position: Two positions with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they are more than 2 arcsec apart; when one states an error radius, the separation is compared with 3 times that radius.
rules.redshift: Two redshifts with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 0.005 (about 1,500 km/s); transient and host redshifts are different definitions and are listed, not compared; host redshifts of differently named hosts are an identity ambiguity.
rules.revision: A retracted row, or a superseded row of the same provider whose value differs beyond the property's rule, is a revision or retraction; a revision within the rule is consistent; the earlier value stays visible.
rules.sigma: Two values that both state an uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 3 combined standard deviations (uncertainties added in quadrature; a stated position error radius is treated as one standard deviation).

evidence_timeline.title: SN II

evidence_timeline.summary: The future of time-domain optical astronomy relies on the development of techniques and software capable of handling a rising amount of data and gradually complementing, or replacing if necessary, real observations. Next-generation surveys, like the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope, will open the door to the new era of optical astrophysics, creating, at the same time, a deficiency in spectroscopic data necessary to confirm the nature of each event and to fully recover the parametric space. In this framework, we developed Core collApse Supernovae parameTers estimatOR (CASTOR), a novel software for data analysis. CASTOR combines Gaussian process and other machine-learning techniques to build time-series templates of synthetic spectra and to estimate parameters of core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) for which only multiband photometry is available. Techniques to build templates are fully data driven and non-parametric through empirical and robust models, and rely on the direct comparison with a training set of 111 CCSNe from the literature. Furthermore, CASTOR employees the real photometric data and the reconstructed synthetic spectra of an event to estimate parameters that belong to the supernova ejecta, to the stellar progenitor and to the event itself, in a rapid and user-friendly framework. In this work, we provide a demonstration of how CASTOR works, studying available data from SN 2015ap and comparing our results with those available in literature.
evidence_timeline.title: Building spectral templates and reconstructing parameters for core-collapse supernovae with CASTOR

evidence_timeline.summary: We present a sample of 34 normal Type II supernovae (SNe II) detected with the Zwicky Transient Facility, with multiband UV light curves starting at t ≤ 4 days after explosion, and X-ray observations. We characterize the early UV-optical color, provide empirical host-extinction corrections, and show that the t > 2 day UV-optical colors and the blackbody evolution of the sample are consistent with shock cooling (SC) regardless of the presence of "flash ionization" features. We present a framework for fitting SC models that can reproduce the parameters of a set of multigroup simulations up to 20% in radius and velocity. Observations of 15 SNe II are well fit by models with breakout radii <10<SUP>14</SUP> cm. Eighteen SNe are typically more luminous, with observations at t ≥ 1 day that are better fit by a model with a large >10<SUP>14</SUP> cm breakout radius. However, these fits predict an early rise during the first day that is too slow. We suggest that these large-breakout events are explosions of stars with an inflated envelope or with confined circumstellar material (CSM). Using the X-ray data, we derive constraints on the extended (∼10<SUP>15</SUP> cm) CSM density independent of spectral modeling and find that most SN II progenitors lose <inline-formula> <mml:math overflow="scroll"><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>̇</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo><</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.25em"></mml:mspace><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>yr</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math> </inline-formula> up to a few years before explosion. We show that the overall observed breakout radius distribution is skewed to higher radii due to a luminosity bias. We argue that the <inline-formula> <mml:math overflow="scroll"><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>66</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>22</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>11</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>%</mml:mo></mml:math> </inline-formula> of red supergiants (RSGs) explode as SNe II with breakout radii consistent with the observed distribution of RSGs, with a tail extending to large radii, likely due to the presence of CSM.
evidence_timeline.title: The Early Ultraviolet Light Curves of Type II Supernovae and the Radii of Their Progenitor Stars

evidence_timeline.summary: Narrow transient emission lines (flash-ionization features) in early supernova (SN) spectra trace the presence of circumstellar material (CSM) around the massive progenitor stars of core-collapse SNe. The lines disappear within days after the SN explosion, suggesting that this material is spatially confined, and originates from enhanced mass loss shortly (months to a few years) prior to the explosion. We performed a systematic survey of H-rich (Type II) SNe discovered within less than 2 days from the explosion during the first phase of the Zwicky Transient Facility survey (2018-2020), finding 30 events for which a first spectrum was obtained within <2 days from the explosion. The measured fraction of events showing flash-ionization features (>36% at the 95% confidence level) confirms that elevated mass loss in massive stars prior to SN explosion is common. We find that SNe II showing flash-ionization features are not significantly brighter, nor bluer, nor more slowly rising than those without. This implies that CSM interaction does not contribute significantly to their early continuum emission, and that the CSM is likely optically thin. We measured the persistence duration of flash-ionization emission and find that most SNe show flash features for ≈5 days. Rarer events, with persistence timescales >10 days, are brighter and rise longer, suggesting these may be intermediate between regular SNe II and strongly interacting SNe IIn.
evidence_timeline.title: The Prevalence and Influence of Circumstellar Material around Hydrogen-rich Supernova Progenitors

evidence_timeline.summary: We report the ZTF discovery of ZTF20ablygyy/2020pni - a rapidly rising young supernova in the nearby galaxy UGC 9684, z=0.01687. The transient was discovered on July 16, 2020 at 04:44 UT with an absolute ZTF r-band magnitude of M = -14.46. A spectrum was obtained with SEDm ~ 1 day after discovery and shows significant He II emission, indicative of strong flash features. We encourage follow-up observations of this transient.
evidence_timeline.title: ZTF early discovery and rapid follow-up of the infant SN ZTF20ablygyy/2020pni
ZTF Transient Classification Report for 2020-07-17

publication_revisions.abstract: The future of time-domain optical astronomy relies on the development of techniques and software capable of handling a rising amount of data and gradually complementing, or replacing if necessary, real observations. Next-generation surveys, like the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope, will open the door to the new era of optical astrophysics, creating, at the same time, a deficiency in spectroscopic data necessary to confirm the nature of each event and to fully recover the parametric space. In this framework, we developed Core collApse Supernovae parameTers estimatOR (CASTOR), a novel software for data analysis. CASTOR combines Gaussian process and other machine-learning techniques to build time-series templates of synthetic spectra and to estimate parameters of core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) for which only multiband photometry is available. Techniques to build templates are fully data driven and non-parametric through empirical and robust models, and rely on the direct comparison with a training set of 111 CCSNe from the literature. Furthermore, CASTOR employees the real photometric data and the reconstructed synthetic spectra of an event to estimate parameters that belong to the supernova ejecta, to the stellar progenitor and to the event itself, in a rapid and user-friendly framework. In this work, we provide a demonstration of how CASTOR works, studying available data from SN 2015ap and comparing our results with those available in literature.
publication_revisions.authors_text: Simongini, Andrea; Ragosta, F.; Piranomonte, S.; Di Palma, I.

publication_revisions.title: Building spectral templates and reconstructing parameters for core-collapse supernovae with CASTOR

publication_revisions.abstract: We present a sample of 34 normal Type II supernovae (SNe II) detected with the Zwicky Transient Facility, with multiband UV light curves starting at t ≤ 4 days after explosion, and X-ray observations. We characterize the early UV-optical color, provide empirical host-extinction corrections, and show that the t > 2 day UV-optical colors and the blackbody evolution of the sample are consistent with shock cooling (SC) regardless of the presence of "flash ionization" features. We present a framework for fitting SC models that can reproduce the parameters of a set of multigroup simulations up to 20% in radius and velocity. Observations of 15 SNe II are well fit by models with breakout radii <10<SUP>14</SUP> cm. Eighteen SNe are typically more luminous, with observations at t ≥ 1 day that are better fit by a model with a large >10<SUP>14</SUP> cm breakout radius. However, these fits predict an early rise during the first day that is too slow. We suggest that these large-breakout events are explosions of stars with an inflated envelope or with confined circumstellar material (CSM). publication_revisions.title: The Early Ultraviolet Light Curves of Type II Supernovae and the Radii of Their Progenitor Stars

publication_revisions.abstract: Narrow transient emission lines (flash-ionization features) in early supernova (SN) spectra trace the presence of circumstellar material (CSM) around the massive progenitor stars of core-collapse SNe. The lines disappear within days after the SN explosion, suggesting that this material is spatially confined, and originates from enhanced mass loss shortly (months to a few years) prior to the explosion. We performed a systematic survey of H-rich (Type II) SNe discovered within less than 2 days from the explosion during the first phase of the Zwicky Transient Facility survey (2018-2020), finding 30 events for which a first spectrum was obtained within <2 days from the explosion. The measured fraction of events showing flash-ionization features (>36% at the 95% confidence level) confirms that elevated mass loss in massive stars prior to SN explosion is common. We find that SNe II showing flash-ionization features are not significantly brighter, nor bluer, nor more slowly rising than those without. This implies that CSM interaction does not contribute significantly to their early continuum emission, and that the CSM is likely optically thin. We measured the persistence duration of flash-ionization emission and find that most SNe show flash features for ≈5 days. Rarer events, with persistence timescales >10 days, are brighter and rise longer, suggesting these may be intermediate between regular SNe II and strongly interacting SNe IIn.

publications.abstract: The future of time-domain optical astronomy relies on the development of techniques and software capable of handling a rising amount of data and gradually complementing, or replacing if necessary, real observations. Next-generation surveys, like the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope, will open the door to the new era of optical astrophysics, creating, at the same time, a deficiency in spectroscopic data necessary to confirm the nature of each event and to fully recover the parametric space. In this framework, we developed Core collApse Supernovae parameTers estimatOR (CASTOR), a novel software for data analysis. CASTOR combines Gaussian process and other machine-learning techniques to build time-series templates of synthetic spectra and to estimate parameters of core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) for which only multiband photometry is available. Techniques to build templates are fully data driven and non-parametric through empirical and robust models, and rely on the direct comparison with a training set of 111 CCSNe from the literature. Furthermore, CASTOR employees the real photometric data and the reconstructed synthetic spectra of an event to estimate parameters that belong to the supernova ejecta, to the stellar progenitor and to the event itself, in a rapid and user-friendly framework. In this work, we provide a demonstration of how CASTOR works, studying available data from SN 2015ap and comparing our results with those available in literature.
